examples.input: I run a local bakery in Austin, TX. I want to rank for 'custom birthday cakes Austin'. My website is basic — a homepage, about page, menu, and contact page. No blog.

output.search_intent: Transactional with local intent — the searcher wants to find and potentially order a custom birthday cake from a bakery in Austin. They need to see designs, pricing, ordering info, and proximity.

recommendations.create_landing_page: Build a dedicated '/custom-birthday-cakes-austin' page — don't try to rank the homepage for this specific query. Include: cake gallery, size/pricing table, ordering process, delivery zones, testimonials, and a clear order CTA.
recommendations.google_business_profile: Optimize your GBP listing: add 'custom birthday cakes' to your business description, upload 10+ photos of birthday cakes, collect reviews that mention 'birthday cake' and 'Austin', post weekly updates with recent cake photos.
recommendations.local_schema: Add LocalBusiness schema with bakery type, address, hours, service area, and price range. Add Product schema for cake categories.
recommendations.content_strategy: Start a simple blog with posts like '10 Custom Birthday Cake Ideas for Kids in Austin', 'How to Order a Custom Cake — Timeline & Tips', 'Gluten-Free Birthday Cake Options at [Bakery Name]'. Each post links to your custom cakes page.
recommendations.technical: Ensure NAP (Name, Address, Phone) is identical on your website, Google Business Profile, Yelp, and all directories. Add an embedded Google Map on your contact page.

examples.input: We have 200 product category pages for our e-commerce store (electronics). They all have thin content — just product grids with no descriptive text. Google Search Console shows 180 of them aren't indexed. How do we fix this?

output.diagnosis: Thin content penalty — Google is choosing not to index pages that provide no unique value beyond a product grid. With 180/200 pages not indexed, this is a site-wide quality signal issue, not just individual page problems.
output.strategy: Don't try to write 200 unique descriptions at once. Prioritize by revenue impact and search volume.

phase_1_top_20.action: Identify the 20 categories with the highest search volume and revenue contribution. Write 300-500 word unique descriptions for each.
phase_1_top_20.template: Each category page should include: 1) Category description (what products are in this category, who they're for, key buying considerations), 2) Buying guide snippet (3-5 factors to consider), 3) FAQ section (3-4 common questions about the category), 4) Internal links to related categories and popular products.
phase_1_top_20.example: For 'Wireless Headphones' category: describe the range (earbuds to over-ear), key specs to compare (ANC, battery life, codec support), use cases (commuting, gaming, workouts), price range overview, and link to related categories (Bluetooth Speakers, Gaming Headsets).

phase_2_scale.action: After Phase 1 pages get indexed (2-4 weeks), use a templatized approach for the next 80 categories. Each gets: 150-200 words of unique content + FAQ schema + breadcrumb schema.
phase_2_scale.warning: Do NOT use AI to generate 200 identical-sounding descriptions. Google detects template content. Each description needs at least 40% unique, category-specific content.

phase_3_remaining.action: For the lowest-priority 100 categories, consider whether they need to be indexed at all. If a category has <5 products and <10 monthly searches, it may be better to noindex it and consolidate into a parent category.

technical_fixes: Add breadcrumb schema to all category pages
Ensure proper canonicalization (no duplicate pages from sort/filter URLs)
Submit an updated sitemap after content additions
Check for faceted navigation creating thousands of crawlable URL combinations — implement proper canonical tags or robots directives
